script:
Now turn to Part three. You will hear a student, Owen, discussing a project with his tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
— Come in, both of you. How is the water usage project going?
— Better than last week. We've got the survey back.
— How many responses in the end?
— Eighty-seven. We were hoping for two hundred, but the response rate from the halls was very low.
— Eighty-seven is workable. What did the halls give you?
— Only eleven. The rest came from the family housing. That's the thing we should say in the write-up, isn't it? That the sample isn't the campus, it's the family housing.
— It is, and say it early rather than in a footnote. Now, what did you find?
— The headline is that people who said they were most concerned about water used the most. Which is the opposite of what we expected.
— Careful. Used the most in total, or the most per person?
— In total.
— And the family households are bigger.
— Ah. So the concerned people might just be the people with more children.
— That's what I'd want you to check before you write that sentence. Divide by household size and see whether it survives.
— If it doesn't survive, do we still report it?
— You report both. The raw figure and the per-person one, and you say which you think is the right unit and why. What you must not do is report only the one that makes the better story.
— Fine. Then the second finding is about the shower timers. We handed out fifty and got thirty-one back with the diaries filled in.
— That's a good return.
— The average shower fell from nine minutes to six in the first week. But by week four it was back to eight.
— That pattern is more interesting than the first-week figure, and it is the one people leave out. Why do you think it drifts back?
— We asked. The most common answer was that they stopped looking at it.
— Then say that, and say how you know. Now, timing. Your draft is due on the nineteenth?
— The twenty-second.
— Even better. Get the per-person recalculation done first, because if the first finding does not survive it, your whole introduction changes and there is no point polishing it before then.
— One last thing. Should we put the diaries in an appendix?
— Put a sample in, not all thirty-one. Three or four that show the range, and say how you chose them.
— Chose them how?
— However you like, as long as you say it. A reader can forgive a small sample and cannot forgive not knowing how it was picked.

items.stem: Water project — number of survey responses:
items.rationale: The figure is given against the target the students hoped for, so two numbers compete in one exchange.

items.stem: Water project — responses from the halls:
items.rationale: The small figure is the reason for the tutor's advice about describing the sample.

items.stem: What does the tutor say about the sample?
options: Describe it early, not in a footnote
items.rationale: The student proposes saying it in the write-up and the tutor adds where it should appear.

items.stem: Why might the headline finding be misleading?
items.rationale: The tutor's question about totals versus per person leads the student to the household-size explanation.

items.stem: Water project — what the tutor asks them to divide by:
items.rationale: The instruction is the practical outcome of the exchange about units.

items.stem: What does the tutor say about reporting the two figures?
options: Report both and justify the unit
items.rationale: He states that both go in with a reason, and names the thing they must not do.

items.stem: Water project — timers returned with diaries:
items.rationale: Two numbers appear together, the number handed out and the number returned.

items.stem: Water project — average shower length in week four:
items.rationale: Three durations appear in sequence and the question asks for the last of them.

items.stem: Why does the tutor find the drift interesting?
items.rationale: He calls the pattern more interesting than the first-week figure and the one people leave out.

items.stem: Water project — date the draft is due:
items.rationale: The tutor names a wrong date and the student corrects him, so the answer is the correction.

script:
Now turn to Part three. You will hear a student, Ines, talking to her tutor about a reading list. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
— So, the reading list. You said it was too long.
— It's forty items for eight weeks. Nobody reads forty items.
— Nobody is meant to. Did you notice it is in three sections?
— I saw the headings, but I assumed they were topics.
— They are not. The first eight are essential, the next twelve are recommended, and the rest is there if you write on that topic.
— That is not obvious from the document.
— No, and that is fair criticism. I will put a sentence at the top before next year. What made you read it as one list?
— The numbering. It runs from one to forty straight through, so it looks like a single sequence.
— That is a good point and an easy fix.
— Can I ask about the two book chapters in the essential eight? The library has one copy of each.
— Both are scanned. They are in the module folder, not the library catalogue, which is probably why you didn't find them.
— I looked in the catalogue for an hour.
— Then that is the second thing I need to fix. Now, about the essay. You are choosing between the migration topic and the housing one?
— Housing, I think. There's more written on it.
— There is more written on it, which cuts both ways. It is easier to find sources and harder to say anything that has not been said.
— Would you steer us away from it?
— No. I would steer you towards a narrower version of it. Housing in general has been done. Housing policy in one city over one decade has not, and it is the same amount of reading.
— That sounds more manageable, actually.
— It usually is. One more thing: the word limit is two thousand, and the penalty above it is steep — five per cent for every hundred words. People lose a grade to that every year, almost always because they left the editing until the last evening.
— Can we use sources that aren't on the list at all?
— Please do. The list is a floor, not a ceiling, and the best essays every year use something I have not read.
— How many extra would you expect?
— I would not put a number on it. Two well-chosen ones are worth ten that are there to lengthen the bibliography, and a marker can tell the difference within a paragraph.
— That's useful. Thank you.

items.stem: Reading list — total number of items:
items.rationale: The number is given alongside the length of the module, so two figures appear together.

items.stem: Reading list — number of essential items:
items.rationale: Three quantities are given in one sentence describing the three sections.

items.stem: Why did the students read it as one list?
options: It was printed on one page
items.rationale: The student identifies the continuous numbering and the tutor accepts it as a good point.

items.stem: Where are the two scanned chapters?
items.rationale: The tutor names the location and explains why the catalogue search failed.

items.stem: Reading list — how long the student searched the catalogue:
items.rationale: The duration is the student's complaint and prompts the tutor's second admission.

items.stem: What does the tutor say about the housing topic?
items.rationale: He says more written on it cuts both ways, easier to source and harder to be original.

items.stem: What does the tutor recommend?
options: A narrower version of the topic
items.rationale: He declines to steer them away and steers them towards a narrower framing instead.

items.stem: Reading list — the narrower framing suggested:
items.prompt: Housing policy in one city over one ___
items.rationale: The narrowing is expressed as two limits, a place and a period, and the item asks for the second.

items.stem: Reading list — the essay word limit:
items.rationale: The limit is stated and then the penalty rate follows, which is the second number.

items.stem: Reading list — penalty for exceeding the limit:
items.prompt: ___ per cent for every hundred words
items.rationale: The rate is described as steep before it is given, which draws attention to the sentence.

script:
Now turn to Part three. You will hear a student, Danny, discussing a work placement with his course tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
— Sit down. You wanted to talk about the placement.
— Yes. I've had two offers and I can't decide.
— Tell me about them.
— The first is a small architecture practice, six people, in the city centre. The second is a large engineering consultancy in Bristol, employing about four hundred professional staff.
— And the work?
— At the small practice I'd be doing a bit of everything. Drawings, site visits, some client meetings. At the large firm I'd be in one team, working on drainage.
— Which one are you leaning towards?
— The small one, because it sounds more interesting. But everyone tells me the big name looks better afterwards.
— Let me push back on that. Whose name is on your degree certificate?
— The university's.
— And who reads your placement report?
— My supervisor here.
— So the name matters less than you have been told. What matters considerably more is what you can describe in an interview, and somebody who has attempted five different activities explains them more convincingly than somebody who has perfected one.
— That's an odd way to put it.
— It is, and it is not quite what I mean. I mean that breadth gives you more to say. But there is a serious argument on the other side, and you should hear it properly. Drainage is unglamorous, and it is simultaneously where the money is, so a summer of specialisation makes you employable in a way that a summer of variety does not.
— So you are saying both.
— I am saying the question is not which is better. It is which one you would still be glad of in two years. Now, some practical things. Are they both paid?
— The large firm pays. The small one offers expenses only.
— Then that is a substantial difference, and you should not pretend otherwise. How far away is Bristol for you?
— An hour and a half each way.
— Three hours a day. Add that up over ten weeks before you decide.
— I hadn't.
— Most people haven't. One last thing: the placement report is due two weeks after you finish, not at the start of term. People miss that every year.
— Should I tell the one I turn down straight away?
— Yes, and this week. They will have a second choice waiting and it is a small profession. A late refusal is remembered longer than a quick one.
— And do I say why?
— A sentence is plenty. You do not owe anybody a paragraph, and a long explanation usually reads as an apology for a decision that needed none.

items.stem: Placement — size of the small practice:
items.rationale: Two staff numbers appear in the same turn, one for each employer.

items.stem: Placement — the specialism at the large firm:
items.rationale: The word is used twice, once in the description and once in the tutor's counter-argument.

items.stem: Placement — what the tutor asks about the degree:
items.prompt: Whose name is on the degree ___
items.rationale: The tutor argues by two questions and the first turns on the document itself.

items.stem: What does the tutor say breadth gives you?
items.rationale: He corrects his own phrasing and settles on breadth giving you more to say.

items.stem: What is the case for the large firm?
items.rationale: He describes drainage as unglamorous and where the money is, making a summer of it valuable.

items.stem: Placement — the tutor's reframing of the question:
items.prompt: Which one you would still be glad of in ___ years
items.rationale: The reframing is the tutor's central advice and carries the only number in that turn.

items.stem: What does the small practice offer instead of pay?
items.rationale: The two arrangements are contrasted directly and the tutor then refuses to call the difference small.

items.stem: Placement — daily travel time to Bristol:
items.rationale: The student gives the one-way time and the tutor doubles it, so the answer is the tutor's figure.

items.stem: Placement — length of the placement:
items.rationale: The duration appears inside the advice about adding up the travelling.

items.stem: When is the placement report due?
items.rationale: The tutor gives the deadline and names the wrong assumption people make every year.

script:
Now turn to Part three. You will hear a student, Priya, planning a presentation with her tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.
— How far have you got with the presentation?
— We have collected the material. My partner and I cannot agree about the structure.
— Go on.
— I want to start with the case study and draw the theory out of it, but my partner wants the theory first. My anxiety is that beginning with a single institution will persuade the audience that the entire presentation concerns that institution.
— That is a genuine risk, and there is a compromise available. Open with two minutes of the case study, pause deliberately, identify the questions it raises, and then move to the theoretical material. You keep the attention and you keep the framing.
— That would work. How long have we got?
— Fifteen minutes and five for questions, and the fifteen is enforced. I stop people at fifteen.
— Even mid-sentence?
— Especially mid-sentence. It is the only way it stays fair.
— How many slides is sensible?
— That is the wrong question entirely. The better question concerns how many ideas, and the answer is approximately four. Some presenters use twenty slides for four ideas and others use precisely four, and either approach can succeed.
— We had thirty-one.
— Then you have more than four ideas, or you have four ideas and a lot of decoration.
— Mostly graphs.
— Graphs are the commonest decoration of all. Interrogate each one about whether the audience can genuinely read it during the six seconds it remains visible. Otherwise it belongs in a handout rather than a presentation.
— Should we hand anything out?
— One page, afterwards, never before. Before, and they read it instead of listening.
— And who speaks when?
— That remains your decision, although you should not alternate at every slide. Two extended turns outperform eight abbreviated ones, because every handover costs the audience approximately ten seconds of concentration.
— What about the questions? Neither of us is confident there.
— Agree in advance who takes what. If a question arrives that neither of you can answer, say so and offer to follow up. The worst answer in a presentation is a confident invention, and the panel always knows.
— Do you want us to rehearse it in front of you?
— I would rather you rehearsed it in front of somebody who does not know the subject. I will nod along at things that are not clear, because I already know what you mean.
— That is a fair point.
— Find a flatmate, and ask them afterwards what the four ideas were. If they can only name two, you have your answer about the slides.

items.stem: What do the students disagree about?
items.rationale: One wants the case study first and the other the theory, which is a disagreement about shape.

items.stem: Presentation — length of the opening case study:
items.prompt: Open with ___ minutes of the case study
items.rationale: The tutor's compromise carries a specific duration among several other numbers in the passage.

items.stem: Presentation — time allowed for questions:
items.rationale: Two durations are given together and the enforcement remark attaches to the first.

items.stem: What does the tutor say about the time limit?
items.rationale: He confirms the interruption and justifies it as the only fair method.

items.stem: Presentation — how many ideas a talk should carry:
items.rationale: The tutor replaces the students' question about slides with this figure, which then recurs.

items.stem: Presentation — number of slides the students had:
items.rationale: The figure is offered by the students and is the trigger for the tutor's diagnosis.

items.stem: What test does the tutor apply to a graph?
options: Whether it reads in six seconds
items.rationale: He gives a specific readability test and says a failing graph belongs in a handout.

items.stem: Presentation — size of the handout:
items.rationale: The instruction carries a quantity and a timing, and the item asks for the quantity.

items.stem: Presentation — attention lost at each handover:
items.rationale: The cost of switching speakers is quantified, which is what makes the advice concrete.

items.stem: What does the tutor call the worst answer?
items.rationale: He names it directly and adds that the panel always knows.
